title: Northern Irish 16-year-olds combine strong place belonging with divided community confidence, heavy social-media exposure, and selective political agency
source_unit: ARK, Northern Ireland Young Life and Times Survey 2026
geography: Northern Ireland; 16-year-olds invited from across the region

observations.period: March 30-May 1, 2026; belonging, community relations, and perceived social openness

denominator.unit: 16-year-olds who took part in the Northern Ireland Young Life and Times Survey

place_belonging.unit: percent definitely or probably expecting to have a sense of belonging to Northern Ireland

community_respect.unit: percent agreeing or strongly agreeing that Northern Ireland is a place where people respect each other

religion_and_relations.unit: percent saying religion will always make a difference to how people in Northern Ireland feel about each other

racist_exposure.unit: percent seeing or hearing racist comments or jokes very or quite often

refugee_openness.value: 34% agree Northern Ireland welcomes refugees escaping persecution, 57% agree it is a duty to protect them, and 67% say media negatively affect perceptions of refugees

meaning_mechanism.value: young people can feel attachment to place while perceiving weak interpersonal respect and frequent prejudice; belonging is therefore not equivalent to social cohesion or inclusive safety

observations.method: ARK Young Life and Times Survey 2026 summary of results; the survey invited 16-year-olds with January-March birthdays across Northern Ireland. Results are self-reported perceptions and experiences, and the 2026 instrument was split across two versions.
observations.uncertainty: Participation is not necessarily a probability sample of all Northern Irish 16-year-olds; item denominators may differ because of the split survey, and perceived exposure does not measure independently verified incidents or causal drivers.
observations.subgroup: Northern Irish 16-year-olds by religion, gender, family affluence, urban/rural setting, school type, and identity context.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strong place belonging may itself be a resource for future civic repair; low respect agreement may reflect strict wording or adolescent skepticism rather than absence of everyday cooperation.

observations.period: 2026; social-media time, platform reach, and online harm among 16-year-olds

denominator.unit: YLT 2026 respondents; individual social-media items may use the relevant split-survey denominator

daily_time.value: 45% report 3-5 hours per day on social media, 24% 6-8 hours, 9% more than 8 hours, and 19% fewer than 3 hours

platform_reach.value: Snapchat 89%, TikTok 87%, Instagram 79%, YouTube 70%, WhatsApp 68%, and Facebook 29% are reported as used

harm_exposure.value: 54% report none of the listed social-media harms; among reported harms, offensive material is 24%, non-consensual sharing of information/photos/videos 16%, and deliberate dishonesty for financial or personal benefit 16%

gendered_exposure.value: girls are more likely than boys to report relationship manipulation (12% versus 8%) and stalking of activities (16% versus 11%)

attention_mechanism.value: high platform exposure coexists with privacy, manipulation, fraud, and harassment risks; social media is both everyday infrastructure and a site where trust and safety costs are unevenly distributed

observations.method: ARK YLT 2026 summary tables on social-media time, apps, and reported harmful behaviours; the measures are survey self-reports, not device logs, content audits, or platform prevalence estimates.
observations.uncertainty: The summary does not provide all item-level response rates, exposure duration definitions, weighting details, or causal ordering; reported harms may be underreported or interpreted differently across respondents.
observations.subgroup: Northern Irish 16-year-olds using Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, WhatsApp, Facebook, and other platforms, with gender and urban/rural differences in exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Heavy use can support friendship, identity, and information access; the harm list captures selected negative experiences and should not be read as net platform effect or inevitable damage.

observations.period: 2026; youth political agency, safety, and environmental meaning

denominator.unit: YLT 2026 respondents; political and environment items may use the relevant split-survey denominator

voting_age.unit: percent in favour of lowering the voting age to 16; 32% opposed and 28% did not know

affluence_difference.value: support for lowering the voting age was 46% among respondents describing their families as not well-off, compared with 40% among average and well-off groups

local_safety.unit: percent feeling fairly or very safe in the area where they lived; very-safe responses were higher in rural than urban areas (55% versus 29%)

nature_values_action.value: 87% agree they treat nature with respect, 82% say being in nature makes them very happy, but only 39% agree they feel part of nature; 70% frequently or more often try to avoid disturbing wildlife

agency_mechanism.value: youth political and ecological agency is selective and situated: support for voice and care for nature coexist with uneven safety, place, and household-resource conditions

observations.method: ARK YLT 2026 summary of political, safety, and environment results; this observation keeps stated support, perceived safety, values, and reported behaviour as separate measures.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not establish future voting, political participation, conservation impact, or causal effects of affluence and geography; the voting-age measure is an attitude, not a turnout or policy outcome.
observations.subgroup: Northern Irish 16-year-olds by family affluence, gender, urban/rural residence, religion, and local safety experience.
observations.counterinterpretation: High environmental values and place safety may support durable participation even where formal political support is uncertain; reported nature behaviour may be constrained by access rather than motivation.

boundary: This record adds a public youth-survey route from place belonging and community tension through social-media exposure, online harm, safety, political agency, and environmental meaning. It is a Northern Ireland 16-year-old survey with a split instrument and self-reported measures; it does not establish causal effects, population-wide prevalence beyond the survey frame, future voting, platform telemetry, independently verified harm, or durable social cohesion.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: ARK YLT 2026 index, summary PDF, and technical-notes PDF were reviewed for fieldwork dates, respondent count, split-survey design, community relations, refugee attitudes, social-media time and harms, political agency, safety, and environmental measures.
